strengths: The paper presents an interesting and timely system: an any-to-any multimodal model that jointly models text, image, and speech discrete tokens under a single mask-based discrete diffusion objective, rather than bolting diffusion decoders onto an autoregressive LLM. This is a meaningful architectural exploration direction.

The training and inference techniques (attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for image generation, special token pre-infilling and adaptive token-length assignment for speech) are practical and well-motivated, and the construction of a Speech-Driven Visual Interaction (SDVI) dataset enables cross-modal speech-visual tasks.

Empirical results are reasonably broad: ASR/TTS (WER on LibriSpeech/LibriTTS), VQA (POPE, MME-Perception, Seed-2-Plus), text-to-image (CLIP-T/CLIP-I), and speech-to-image alignment. The model is competitive with or better than AnyGPT/NExT-GPT and approaches specialized models, which supports the feasibility claim.

The sampling-efficiency study (Tab. 3, Fig. 7) and the training-free inpainting capability are convincing demonstrations of advantages specific to the diffusion formulation, and qualitative figures show genuine speech-to-image and spoken visual dialogue behavior.
Implementation details (backbone Dream-7B-Instruct, tokenizers, dataset composition in Tab. 4, hyperparameters) are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim of being 'the first any-to-any multimodal language model built on mask-based discrete diffusion' is questionable. The paper itself cites Lumina-DiMOO [43], an 'omni diffusion large language model for multi-modal generation and understanding,' as well as MMaDA [45] and Dimple [51], which are multimodal diffusion LLMs. The paper does not clearly articulate what differentiates Omni-Diffusion from these systems or why the 'first' claim holds; this needs to be substantiated or softened.

There are no ablation studies for any of the proposed techniques. The contributions of attenuated tail-pad masking (vs. uniform masking), position penalty, special token pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length assignment are asserted but never quantified. Given that these are listed as core contributions, this is a significant evidential gap.

Image generation is evaluated only with CLIP-T/CLIP-I on MSCOCO. No FID/GenEval/human evaluation is reported, and CLIP scores are known to be a weak proxy for visual quality. The comparison table also mixes self-run evaluations ('*') with numbers copied from prior papers, and several baseline cells are missing, making comparisons uneven.

The narrative of a 'unified joint distribution over multimodal discrete tokens' is not fully accurate for speech understanding: speech input is encoded by an external SenseVoiceSmall encoder with continuous features projected via an MLP adapter, not discretized tokens; only speech output uses discrete tokens via the GLM-4-Voice decoder. This asymmetric design weakens the claim of an intrinsically aligned discrete semantic space and deserves explicit discussion.

Quantitative evaluation of the speech-driven visual interaction capability (the headline multi-modality scenario) is thin: speech-to-image is measured only via CLIP scores on synthesized speech, and spoken visual QA is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 4). No benchmark numbers are given for the SDVI tasks the dataset was built for.

Some baselines appear outdated or weak for 2026 standards (e.g., mPLUG-Owl, LLaVA-1, InstructBLIP), and recent comparable diffusion-based unified models (MMaDA, Lumina-DiMOO, Dimple) are absent from the experimental comparisons.

No code or model release is mentioned, no limitations section is included, and Table 4 contains an obvious duplication error (JourneyDB listed twice), suggesting insufficient polish. The 2000K 'In-house Dataset' for visual QA is not described at all, hurting reproducibility and transparency.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and timely direction: building an any-to-any multimodal system on a mask-based discrete diffusion backbone rather than an autoregressive LLM, and the unified mask-token prediction formulation over text, image, and speech tokens is cleanly presented (Sec. 3.1).

The system covers an unusually broad task suite — ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual QA, and zero-shot inpainting — and the sampling-efficiency analysis (Tab. 3, Fig. 7) showing graceful degradation down to ~10 inference steps is a concrete demonstration of the parallel-decoding advantage of diffusion.

Several inference-time techniques (position penalty, special token pre-infilling, adaptive token-length assignment) are thoughtful adaptations that exploit properties specific to masked diffusion models rather than direct transfers from AR systems.
Implementation details, training hyperparameters, and the dataset composition (Tab. 4) are reported in a reasonably complete appendix.
weaknesses: Missing ablations undermine the central technical claims. The four proposed techniques — attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special token pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length assignment — are each justified only by qualitative reasoning; no experiment isolates their contribution, and it is unclear how much of the reported performance comes from the strong Dream-7B initialization and off-the-shelf tokenizers (MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, GLM-4-Voice decoder) versus the novel components.

The 'first any-to-any multimodal model built on masked discrete diffusion' claim is not adequately established. Concurrent/related systems (MMada [45], Dimple [51], Lumina-DiMOO [43], NExT-Omni [27]) already combine diffusion LMs with multimodal understanding and generation; the related-work section dismisses these too briefly, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is genuinely new beyond the speech modality and specific inference tricks.

Evaluation is weak for the headline claims. Text-to-image quality is judged only by CLIP-T/CLIP-I, which are known to be poor proxies for image quality and prompt fidelity (no FID, no human evaluation); the VQA baselines (LLaVA, mPLUG-Owl, InstructBLIP) are 2023-era models that are far below the current state of the art, making 'comparable to specialized visual LLMs' an overstated comparison; and in Tab. 2 the method is actually below Emu on both CLIP metrics, which sits uneasily with the abstract's claim of 'outperforms or performs on par'.

The SDVI dataset is small (30K samples per task), synthesized entirely with CosyVoice2 voice cloning, and not shown to be released, so the flagship speech-driven visual interaction capability rests on a narrow, noisy data foundation; no code, model, or data release is stated, hurting reproducibility.

There is no evaluation of core text or language capability after multimodal training — a critical question when replacing an AR LLM with a diffusion backbone in a unified model is whether the base LM competence degrades; the absence of any text benchmark or limitation discussion on this point is a notable gap.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: multiple typos ('regidly', 'tipically', 'Speech-Diven', 'LLaVA-OneVisual'), a broken/absent project webpage link in the abstract, a duplicated row in Tab. 4 (JourneyDB listed twice), and inconsistent baseline reporting (missing cells, mixed starred/unstarred evaluation protocols) make careful reading difficult.
No limitations section and no discussion of research ethics (e.g., voice cloning data provenance for SDVI, potential misuse of speech synthesis), which ICML submissions are expected to address.

strengths: The core idea — a genuinely unified any-to-any multimodal model whose backbone is a mask-based discrete diffusion model over joint discrete token distributions of text, image, and speech — is a promising and relatively unexplored architectural direction, and the paper demonstrates it is feasible at 7B scale with non-trivial results.

The set of adapted techniques is thoughtful and well-motivated: attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty to mitigate the well-known ends-toward-center decoding pathology, special token pre-infilling for spoken dialogue, and adaptive token-length initialization for ASR/TTS. These exploit properties unique to diffusion models rather than being generic.

Evaluation spans a reasonably broad task suite (ASR/TTS WER on LibriSpeech/LibriTTS, VQA on POPE/MME/Seed-2-Plus, CLIP-T/CLIP-I on MSCOCO, speech-to-image alignment, inpainting, and few-step sampling), and the model is competitive with or better than any-to-any AR baselines like AnyGPT on several of them.

The few-step sampling results (Table 3, Fig. 7) are a concrete demonstration of a practical advantage of diffusion backbones over autoregressive ones for multimodal generation, and training-free inpainting is a nice bonus capability.
Hyperparameters, dataset composition (Table 4), and tokenizer choices are documented in the appendix, giving reasonable implementation transparency.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim — 'the first any-to-any multimodal language model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion' — is not adequately defended against closely related work. The paper itself cites MMaDA [45], Dimple [51], and Lumina-DiMOO [43] (described as 'an omni diffusion large language model for multi-modal generation and understanding'), and NExT-Omni [27], yet none of these diffusion-based multimodal models appear as baselines in any experiment. A direct comparison with at least the closest such system is needed to substantiate both the 'first' claim and the performance claims.

No ablation studies are provided for the proposed techniques. The claims that position penalty reduces repetitive patterns, that attenuated tail-pad masking prevents pad-token overfitting, and that special token pre-infilling improves spoken dialogue coherence are supported only by qualitative reasoning and cherry-picked examples (Fig. 4). Quantitative with/without ablations are essential given these are listed as key contributions.

Image generation is evaluated only via CLIP-T/CLIP-I, which are known to be weak proxies for visual quality and prompt fidelity; the paper even acknowledges (Table 2) that models with external pretrained diffusion decoders achieve higher CLIP-I. No FID, human evaluation, ImageReward/HPS, or compositional benchmarks are reported, making the 'visual quality comparable' claim under-supported.

There is no evaluation of the model's retained pure-text language capability after multimodal training. For a model whose selling point is a joint semantic space, showing that text quality did not degrade (e.g., standard LLM benchmarks) is important, especially since diffusion LLM backbones are already weaker than AR LLMs of comparable size.

Several experimental details are missing or ambiguous: how speech understanding (ASR/spoken VQA) interacts with the fixed SenseVoice encoder at inference, the number of VQA tokens, how 'in-house dataset' (2000K samples) was constructed, and how baseline numbers in Tables 1–2 were obtained (some marked '*' as re-evaluations, others apparently copied without clear sourcing).

The paper lacks a limitations discussion and any treatment of data ethics: the SDVI dataset is built via voice cloning with CosyVoice2 on GigaSpeech speakers, and speech is synthesized from LLaVA-OneVision content, with no discussion of speaker consent or synthesis safeguards — a notable omission for a system generating speech.

Presentation quality is below par for a main-track submission: multiple typos ('tipically', 'regidly', 'Speech-Diven', 'LLaVA-OneVisual' vs OneVision), a cluttered Figure 1 with duplicated tokens ('A2: A2:', 'Q2:'), inconsistent naming (Seed-2-Plus vs Seed-Bench-2-Plus), and Common Voice cited as [29] (LibriSpeech) in Table 4.

Reproducibility is uncertain: a project webpage is referenced but no code, model weights, or SDVI dataset release is clearly stated, and several inference-time heuristics (e.g., the 0.25L pre-infilling split, 3.5x/0.2x length factors) appear tuned without justification, which would hinder others from building on the work reliably.

strengths: The paper presents the first any-to-any multimodal system built entirely on a mask-based discrete diffusion backbone (Dream-7B), which is a meaningful architectural alternative to the dominant LLM-plus-connector paradigm and enables capabilities like zero-shot inpainting and controllable initial mask sequences (special token pre-infilling).

The evaluation is fairly broad for a systems paper: speech (ASR/TTS WER on LibriSpeech/LibriTTS), visual understanding (POPE, MME-P, Seed-2-Plus), text-to-image (CLIP-T/CLIP-I on MSCOCO, DPG-Bench), cross-modal speech-to-image alignment, sampling-efficiency sweeps, and latency comparisons against AR baselines.

The training and inference techniques (attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for decoding-order artifacts, special token pre-infilling, adaptive token-length assignment) are concrete, well-motivated by observed failure modes, and mostly supported by ablations (e.g., Table 6 for position penalty, Figure 8 for pre-infilling).

The SDVI dataset construction pipeline is described in reasonable detail, and the three-stage progressive training pipeline is clearly documented with dataset statistics (Table 4) and hyperparameters in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

Table 3 and Table 8 demonstrate a practically relevant trade-off: near-parity CLIP scores at 10 inference steps (1.29s vs 28.5s at 256 steps), supporting the efficiency argument for diffusion over autoregressive multimodal generation.
weaknesses: The claimed 'first any-to-any' status is on thin ice: related concurrent and prior works (Dimple, NeXT-Omni, Lumina-DiMOO, Fudoki, MMaDA) already apply diffusion-style backbones to multimodal modeling, and the distinction from DFM-based models is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated (no head-to-head comparison with NeXT-Omni).

Baselines are weak or outdated. AnyGPT (ACL 2024) and NExT-GPT (ICML 2024) are the only any-to-any comparators; stronger recent unified models (Qwen3-Omni, VITA-1.5, Show-o variants, LLaDA-V) are cited but not compared on the main benchmarks, making 'comparable or better than existing multimodal systems' an overclaim.

The ASR result (7.05 WER) is actually substantially worse than the speech LLM baseline GLM-4-Voice (2.82), yet the abstract and Section 4.1 describe speech performance as 'comparable' or 'better than existing autoregressive systems' — this is misleading framing of Table 1.

Some ablations are weak or missing. The position penalty ablation (Table 6) shows a negligible CLIP delta (0.233→0.235, 0.666→0.667), and the hypothesized repetitive-pattern mechanism is never quantitatively validated (no FID, no human study, no repetition metric). Special token pre-infilling and adaptive token-length assignment are supported only qualitatively (Figure 8) rather than by controlled quantitative ablations.

Image generation quality is assessed only via CLIP-style metrics; no FID/GenEval/human evaluation. CLIP-T (0.235) is below even the older Emu (0.286), so 'visual quality comparable to methods that rely on external pretrained diffusion models' is not well supported.

The SDVI dataset is small (30K samples each for two tasks) and synthetic (CosyVoice2 voice cloning of LLaVA-OneVision and Blip3o data), raising questions about generalization of the headline speech-driven visual interaction capability; the Spoken VQA evaluation is on a self-converted MME benchmark rather than an established benchmark.

Several claims and presentation details need tightening: the MME-P score (1216.7) barely exceeds InstructBLIP while the model is built on a much stronger 7B diffusion LM; the latency advantage over AR baselines holds only at 10 steps with degraded quality; there are typos ('Speech-Diven', 'RTF caculated', duplicated 'JourneyDB 4000K' row in Table 4) and Table 2 mixes self-reported and re-evaluated numbers inconsistently.

The limitations section is superficial (one sentence about future scaling) and omits known weaknesses evident in the results (ASR gap, image quality gap to dedicated generators, synthetic speech data). No code or model release is confirmed — the project webpage is blank in the manuscript.

strengths: The idea of building an any-to-any multimodal system on a single mask-based discrete diffusion backbone (rather than an AR LLM with detached generation heads) is a reasonable and timely direction, and the paper gives a clear system-level description of the tokenizer choices, three-stage training pipeline, and a constructed SDVI dataset.

The breadth of evaluation is non-trivial for a single system: ASR/TTS (WER on LibriSpeech/LibriTTS), VQA (POPE, MME-P, Seed-2-Plus), text-to-image (CLIP-T/CLIP-I, DPG-Bench), speech-to-image, inpainting, and few-step sampling/latency analyses.

Some inference-time techniques (entropy-based confidence decoding, adaptive token-length initialization exploiting the speech-duration/text-length correlation, special token pre-infilling to expose text semantics during speech generation) are sensible exploitations of the flexibility that mask-based diffusion affords, and the few-step sampling results (Table 3) are a genuinely useful property of this architecture.
The paper is generally readable, and an appendix provides implementation hyperparameters and dataset composition.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim is not well supported. The paper claims to be 'the first any-to-any multimodal language model built on mask-based discrete diffusion,' yet its own related-work section cites several closely related systems (MMaDA, Dimple, LLaDA-V, NeXT-Omni based on discrete flow matching, Lumina-DiMoO). The stated distinction from DFM-based models (loss on masked tokens vs. velocity on the full sequence; top-k freezing) is a training/inference detail rather than a demonstrated conceptual advance, and no head-to-head comparison with NeXT-Omni, MMaDA, or Show-o is provided, which are the most relevant baselines.

The claim of 'comparable to or even better than existing AR-based multimodal systems' rests on comparisons against outdated baselines (LLaVA-1, InstructBLIP, mPLUG-Owl, AnyGPT, NExT-GPT, Emu). Modern MLLMs/omni-models (Qwen-Omni, VITA-1.5, Show-o, MMaDA, BLIP3-o) are far stronger, and their omission makes the competitive positioning claim unsupported.

The 'unified joint modeling' story is undermined by the architecture: speech understanding uses a discriminative SenseVoiceSmall encoder with an MLP adapter, so comprehension of speech is not actually modeled by the diffusion process; only speech generation goes through diffusion tokens. The paper does not acknowledge this asymmetry.

Many results are fragile or within noise: the position-penalty ablation improves CLIP-T by only 0.002 (0.233 vs 0.235) and CLIP-I by 0.001 (Table 6), with no variance, seeds, or significance testing; single-run numbers are reported throughout. No ablation isolates the contribution of the three-stage pipeline vs. single-stage training, and no ablation covers γ, Nt, or the adaptive length constants (3.5x, 0.2x).

Several evaluations are self-constructed and potentially confounded: Spoken VQA is evaluated on MME questions converted by CosyVoice2 — the same synthesis model used to build the training SDVI data — raising train/test pipeline overlap concerns; the speech-to-image alignment evaluation similarly converts MSCOCO captions with CosyVoice2 while CosyVoice2-derived speech was in training data. No external standard benchmark exists for the cross-modal claims, and the 30K-sample SDVI set is small relative to the 10M+ image-text data.

Key supporting evidence for the core claim that joint token modeling yields an 'intrinsically well-aligned semantic representation space' is missing: there is no probing of the shared representation space, no text-only capability retention evaluation after multimodal training (a standard concern when extending a pretrained diffusion LM), and no analysis of whether the alignment claim holds beyond CLIP-style correlations.

The proposed techniques are largely ad hoc heuristics (hard-coded 0.25L pre-infilling position, 3.5x/0.2x length factors, position penalty over the last L-100 tokens with hand-set decay to 0.5), with little analysis of when they fail, sensitivity, or generality across settings — limiting their value as transferable contributions.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model release is evident (project webpage placeholder), the 'in-house dataset' (2000K samples) is unspecified, latency measurements lack hardware/precision details, and text decoding hyperparameters (top-k, number of steps for each reported result) are incompletely specified.

The limitations section is superficial (mentions only future extension to editing/scaling) and does not engage with the substantive limitations above (heuristic dependence, outdated baselines, encoder-based speech understanding). Voice cloning of GigaSpeech speakers for dataset construction is used without any discussion of consent or ethical treatment, and the impact statement is boilerplate.

Presentation issues: repeated typos ('Speech-Diven', 'caculated', 'estimate as'), duplicated text in Figure 1, Table 4 lists 'Librispeech' as the source for 'Common Voice 17', and several sentences in the experiments section restate the same point verbatim, suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely interesting systems contribution: an any-to-any multimodal model (text, image, speech) built entirely on a mask-based discrete diffusion backbone (Dream-7B), which is a relatively underexplored design compared to the dominant LLM-with-decoders paradigm.

A coherent suite of diffusion-specific training and inference techniques is proposed (attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special token pre-infilling, adaptive token length assignment), which are potentially reusable insights for the community working on masked diffusion models.
Evaluation spans multiple modalities (ASR/TTS WER, VQA benchmarks, CLIP-T/CLIP-I for image generation, DPG-Bench, sampling efficiency, inpainting), which is broader than typical bimodal papers.
The construction of a speech-driven visual interaction (SDVI) dataset and the speech-to-image evaluation are a useful addition, as trilingual text-image-speech joint benchmarks are scarce.
The limitations section (Appendix C) is honest about scope, and the paper clearly explains its distinctions from DFM-based models like NeXT-Omni.
weaknesses: The central claim of being 'comparable to or even better than existing autoregressive multimodal systems' is overstated relative to the evidence. Table 2 shows CLIP-T of 0.235, below both DreamLLM (0.238) and Emu (0.286), and the ASR WER of 7.05 in Table 1 is substantially worse than GLM-4-Voice (2.82); describing these as 'comparable' weakens the credibility of the empirical claims.

The closest competitors are missing from the quantitative comparison. NeXT-Omni [30], the DFM-based any-to-any model the paper itself explicitly distinguishes from, and stronger recent systems (Qwen3-Omni, VITA-1.5, Lumina-DiMOO, MMaDA, Dimple) are discussed in related work but never compared with, making the novelty and superiority claims hard to verify.

Ablation evidence for the proposed techniques is thin. The position penalty ablation (Table 6) shows differences of 0.002 CLIP-T and 0.001 CLIP-I, which are within plausible evaluation noise, yet the paper asserts visual quality 'declines' without it; the pre-infilling ablation is purely qualitative. Adaptive token length assignment has no ablation at all.

The efficiency advantage over autoregressive baselines is not convincingly demonstrated: at full 256 steps, image generation latency is 28.5s versus 3.02s for Emu and 6.23s for NeXT-GPT, and the claimed efficiency only materializes at 10 steps where generation quality measurably drops (CLIP-I 0.650 vs 0.667). The latency comparisons also lack detail on hardware and implementation parity.

Key design choices are ad hoc heuristics with weak justification: the pre-infilling split at a fixed 0.25L, the fixed 3.5x/0.2x token length multipliers, and the scale factor gamma = 0.6 are presented without sensitivity analysis.

The claim of being 'the first any-to-any multimodal language model built on mask-based discrete diffusion' requires more careful qualification given prior multimodal diffusion LLMs (MMaDA, Dimple, Lumina-DiMOO, Show-o); the exact delta over these works should be stated precisely.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the project webpage link is blank in the manuscript, and there is no explicit statement about releasing code, model weights, or the SDVI dataset, despite the pipeline depending on many proprietary/patched components (in-house VQA dataset of 2000K samples is not described or released).

The SDVI dataset is small (30K samples) and derived via voice cloning with CosyVoice2 on third-party data (LLaVA-OneVision, Blip3o, GigaSpeech); the ethics of voice cloning and any licensing constraints of the underlying datasets are not discussed, and the impact statement is boilerplate.
The paper does not evaluate whether joint multimodal training degrades the base Dream-7B's text-only language ability, which is an important consideration for any unified foundation model.
